chunks.text: Mr. Septimus Hargreave, the collector, was last seen entering his Curio Room at half past nine on Friday, 27 November 1891. At half past ten the household found the door locked and the key missing. When it was forced at a quarter past eleven the room was empty, the window bolted, and a letter lay on the desk. The letter says Mr. Hargreave has gone abroad. Every suspect has an alibi that seems to hold. This is your final examination, Detective. Combine at least three independent pieces of evidence - words, keys, times and an overlooked document - to show who is responsible. No single document gives the answer.
chunks.title: Case introduction: The Final Deception

chunks.text:
Found on the Curio Room desk beneath a paperweight, in a hand resembling Mr. Hargreave's.

To whom it may concern,

I have gone abroad and shall not return. My cabinet of curiosities is to be placed in the care of my partner, Mr. Black, until it can be sold. Do not search for me.

Septimus Hargreave
chunks.title: The Original Letter on the Desk
chunks.author: Signed "Septimus Hargreave"

chunks.text: PRIVATE DIARY of Septimus Hargreave. Wed 25th. Mrs. Reed called again to ask after the Fenwick jade. She insists it was her husband's. It was not. She calls my collection her "cabinet of curiosities", a phrase I find vulgar; it is the Hargreave Collection, nothing less. I told her I shall settle the matter at the Society on Monday and the jade will go to the museum. Thu 26th.
chunks.title: Mr. Hargreave's Private Diary
chunks.author: Septimus Hargreave

chunks.text: Thu 26th. Black presses me on the Lisbon sale. I refuse. Eleanor has typed my will and I am reassured. Lane writes he will inspect the Roman glass on Saturday. I shall dine alone tomorrow after Black leaves, and work in the Curio Room.
chunks.title: Mr. Hargreave's Private Diary
chunks.author: Septimus Hargreave

chunks.text:
Inspection of the Curio Room, Hargreave House, by Inspector Hollis.

The door was locked and there was no key in the lock. Key A hangs on Mr. Hargreave's watch chain, which lay on the desk inside the room; Key B is absent from the key cabinet. The window is bolted from inside. There is no sign of struggle. The collection is intact. The lamp on the desk is low and a letter lay on the blotter beneath a paperweight. The door was forced at a quarter past eleven.
chunks.title: Curio Room Inspection
chunks.author: Inspector Hollis

chunks.text:
KEY REGISTER - Curio Room keys. Kept by Mr. Ford.

Key A - kept on Mr. Hargreave's watch chain.
Key B - spare, kept in the locked key cabinet in the housekeeper's room.

Friday 27 Nov.
4:00 PM - Key B issued to Mrs. M. Reed, by Mr. Hargreave's permission, to view the jade. (J.F.)
4:30 PM - "Returned. M.R." - entry in Mrs. Reed's hand.
11:20 PM - Key B found absent from the cabinet. (J.F.)
chunks.title: Key Register
chunks.author: Mr. Ford, household manager

chunks.text:
HOUSEHOLD SCHEDULE - Friday 27 November.

4:15 PM - Mr. Ford leaves with the carriage; the key cabinet is locked and its key is with him. 6:00 PM - Mr. Ford returns.
6:00 PM - Mr. Hargreave and Mr. Black dine in the study. Mr. Black leaves at 7:30 PM.
9:00 PM - The garden door is normally bolted. On Fridays it is left unbolted until 10:00 PM for the coal delivery.
9:00 PM - Miss White types in the library.
9:30 PM - Mr. Ford begins night rounds of the ground floor; ends 10:30 PM.
9:30 PM - Mr. Hargreave retires to the Curio Room.
chunks.title: Household Schedule for Friday
chunks.author: Mr. Ford, household manager

chunks.text:
MESSAGES received at Hargreave House, Friday 27 November.

3:40 PM - Telegram from Mr. Lane: "Regret cannot attend this week. Will call Saturday. - Lane."
9:20 PM - Note brought to the front door by an errand boy and carried to the Curio Room by Mr. Ford: "H. - The Fenwick fragment is found. Come to the garden gate at ten, alone, and say nothing to Black. - L."
chunks.title: A Set of Messages
chunks.author: Various

4:00 PM - Mrs. M. Reed in.
5:10 PM - Mrs. M. Reed out, by the front door.

chunks.text:
TIMELINE (draft) of Friday 27 November.

7:30 PM - Mr. Black leaves for his club.
9:30 PM - Mr. Hargreave retires to the Curio Room; Mr. Ford begins night rounds.
9:45 PM - Mr. Ford passes the library; Miss White typing.

11:15 PM - Door forced; room empty; letter on the desk.
Inspector's note: alibis: Black - club to 10:30; White - library 9:00 to 10:30, confirmed by Ford; Ford - rounds, confirmed by White; Lane - Society lecture 8:00 to 10:30; Reed - home in Kensington after six.
chunks.title: Reconstructed Timeline (Inspector's Draft)
chunks.author: Inspector Hollis

chunks.text:
DAWKINS & SON - Coal Merchants. Delivery receipt, 14 Cavendish Row.

Four tons, delivered by the garden door between 9:30 PM and 9:55 PM. The door was open and the cellar-hole clear.
Receipt signed in the master's absence by a lady in a black veil, who gave the carter a half-crown and said the master was not to be disturbed. The carter did not see her face.
chunks.title: Coal Merchant's Delivery Receipt
chunks.author: Messrs. Dawkins & Son, coal merchants

chunks.text:
Statement of Arthur Black.

I dined with Septimus until half past seven and then went to my club, where I remained until half past ten. I know nothing of any letter. I am named in it, and I resent it. I wanted the Lisbon sale and I do not deny it.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Arthur Black
chunks.author: Arthur Black

chunks.text:
Statement of Eleanor White.

I typed in the library from nine until half past ten. Mr. Ford passed the door at a quarter to ten. At about ten I heard faint voices in the garden, which I took for the coalmen. I wear spectacles and have never worn a veil.
chunks.title: Statement of Miss Eleanor White
chunks.author: Eleanor White

chunks.text:
Statement of James Ford.

I issued Key B to Mrs. Reed at four o'clock and left with the carriage at a quarter past four. I carried a note to Mr.
Hargreave at twenty past nine. I did my rounds from half past nine to half past ten and passed the library at a quarter to ten. I saw no lady that night. Mrs. Reed, as ever in her widow's veil, is the only lady of our acquaintance who wears one.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. James Ford
chunks.author: James Ford

chunks.text:
Statement of Victor Lane.

I sent a telegram that afternoon saying I could not attend that week. I was at the Antiquarian Society's lecture from eight until half past ten. I sent no note to Mr. Hargreave and wrote nothing to anyone about a garden gate.
chunks.title: Statement of Mr. Victor Lane
chunks.author: Victor Lane

chunks.text:
Statement of Margaret Reed.

I left Cavendish Row at ten past five and was at home in Kensington by six. I dined alone and retired early with a headache.
I wrote in the register that I had returned the key. I know nothing of any letter.
chunks.title: Statement of Mrs. Margaret Reed
chunks.author: Margaret Reed

chunks.text: Arthur Black, Hargreave's business partner. Background: Co-owner of Hargreave & Black, Antiquaries. Impatient with Hargreave's reluctance to sell the collection. Practical, blunt, with a reputation for hard bargains. Motive: Wanted the Lisbon sale of the collection; Hargreave kept refusing. Relationship: Business partner of Septimus Hargreave. Known whereabouts: Dined with Mr. Hargreave until half past seven, then at his club until half past ten.
chunks.title: Profile of Arthur Black

chunks.text: Personality: Blunt, impatient, answers directly and bluntly, dislikes riddles. He dined with Hargreave in the study until 7:30 and then went to his club, where he stayed until 10:30. He was named in the letter, which surprised and angered him. He did not write it. Does not know: Who wrote the letter.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Arthur Black

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you on Friday night? Where were you at ten? Where were you at 9:45? Answer: At my club from about eight until half past ten. The porter and half the members saw me. I dined with Septimus until half past seven first.
chunks.title: Arthur Black on: Where were you on Friday night

chunks.text: Questions: Do you have a motive? Did you want the collection sold? Why does the letter name you? Answer: I wanted the Lisbon sale, yes, and he refused, yes. I am named in the letter because someone wants me blamed. I did not write it.
chunks.title: Arthur Black on: Do you have a motive

chunks.text: Questions: Who has keys to the Curio Room? Who had access to the key cabinet? Answer: Septimus carries one. The spare is in the cabinet, which Ford keeps. I never touched either.
chunks.title: Arthur Black on: Who has keys to the Curio Room

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Eleanor, James, Victor or Margaret? Answer: I will not slander the household. I will say Mrs. Reed was forever after that jade.
chunks.title: Arthur Black on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Eleanor White, Hargreave's personal secretary. Background: Hargreave's secretary for four years. Neat, quick and discreet, wears spectacles, and is quietly proud that the master trusts her with his will. Motive: Named in Hargreave's will; but she gains nothing from his disappearance that she would not have gained otherwise. Relationship: Personal secretary of Septimus Hargreave. Known whereabouts: Typing letters in the library from nine until half past ten; Ford passed at a quarter to ten.
chunks.title: Profile of Eleanor White

chunks.text: Personality: Precise, quiet, slightly formal, reports exactly what she heard and saw. She typed in the library from nine to half past ten. She heard Ford pass at a quarter to ten and also heard faint voices in the garden at about ten, which she did not investigate. She does not wear a veil. Does not know: Who wrote the letter.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Eleanor White

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at nine? Where were you at ten? What were you doing? Answer: In the library, typing the week's letters from nine until half past ten. Mr. Ford passed the door at a quarter to ten.
chunks.title: Eleanor White on: Where were you at nine

chunks.text: Questions: Did you hear anything? Did you hear voices in the garden? What did you notice? Answer: At about ten I heard faint voices in the garden, I believe two. I thought the coalmen. I did not look.
chunks.title: Eleanor White on: Did you hear anything

chunks.text: Questions: Do you wear a veil? Who wears a veil? Is there a lady with a veil? Answer: I wear spectacles, not a veil. Mrs. Reed is the only lady of our acquaintance who wears a veil; she is in widow's weeds.
chunks.title: Eleanor White on: Do you wear a veil

chunks.text: Questions: What does the will say? Do you benefit? Do you have a motive? Answer: I am remembered in the will, but a small sum. I would have more by his staying alive.
chunks.title: Eleanor White on: What does the will say

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Arthur, James, Victor or Margaret? Answer: I have no evidence. Mr. Black is angry, Mrs. Reed is persistent, Mr. Lane is a scholar. That is all I can say.
chunks.title: Eleanor White on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: James Ford, the household manager. Background: Hargreave's household manager for fifteen years. Keeper of the keys, schedules and registers. Meticulous, loyal, anxious about being blamed for a missing key. Motive: None known; devoted to his master. Relationship: Household manager and keeper of the key register. Known whereabouts: On the carriage from 4:15 to 6:00 PM; on night rounds of the ground floor from 9:30 to 10:30 PM.
chunks.title: Profile of James Ford

chunks.text: Personality: Formal, orderly, quotes the register, fussy about times. He issued Key B to Mrs. Reed at 4:00 PM for the jade and left with the carriage at 4:15 PM. He did not check the cabinet afterwards. At 9:20 he carried a note delivered by a boy to the Curio Room. He did night rounds from 9:30 to 10:30 and passed the library at a quarter to ten. He never saw a lady in a veil. He knows Mrs. Reed wears a veil. Does not know: What the note said.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of James Ford

chunks.text: Questions: Who had the key? Who took Key B? Who returned the key? Answer: I issued Key B to Mrs. Reed at four o'clock to view the jade. The register says she returned it at half past four, in her own hand. I had left with the carriage at a quarter past four.
chunks.title: James Ford on: Who had the key

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at 9:45? What were your rounds? Where were you at ten? Answer: On my night rounds of the ground floor from half past nine to half past ten. I passed the library at a quarter to ten and heard Miss White typing.
chunks.title: James Ford on: Where were you at 9:45

chunks.text: Questions: Did you deliver a note to Mr. Hargreave? What was the note? Who sent it? Answer: At twenty past nine a boy brought a note and I carried it to the Curio Room myself. I do not know what it said.
chunks.title: James Ford on: Did you deliver a note to Mr. Hargreave

chunks.text: Questions: Was the garden door open? Who had access to the garden door? What about the coal delivery? Answer: The garden door is bolted at nine on every night but Friday, when the coalmen come, and it was unbolted until ten.
chunks.title: James Ford on: Was the garden door open

chunks.text: Questions: Does Mrs. Reed wear a veil? Who wears a veil? Did you see a lady? Answer: Mrs. Reed always wears her widow's veil. I saw no lady that night, sir, on my rounds.
chunks.title: James Ford on: Does Mrs. Reed wear a veil

chunks.text: Victor Lane, a visiting historian. Background: A historian of Roman glass who was to inspect the collection on Saturday. Pleasant, forgetful, absorbed in his work. Motive: Hoped to be allowed to publish the collection's catalogue. Relationship: Visiting scholar and correspondent of Septimus Hargreave. Known whereabouts: At a lecture of the Antiquarian Society from eight until half past ten.
chunks.title: Profile of Victor Lane

chunks.text: Personality: Genial, absent-minded, anxious to be helpful, apt to ramble. He sent a telegram that afternoon saying he could not attend that week and would call on Saturday. He was at a lecture of the Antiquarian Society, where the Secretary can vouch for him. He sent no note to the garden gate. Does not know: Who forged his initial.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Victor Lane

chunks.text: Questions: Did you send a note? Did you write the note signed L? Did you ask Mr. Hargreave to the garden gate? Answer: I sent only a telegram, that afternoon, to say I could not come that week. I did not send any note. Someone has used my initial.
chunks.title: Victor Lane on: Did you send a note

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at ten? Where were you that night? Answer: At the Antiquarian Society's lecture from eight until half past ten. The Secretary will vouch for me.
chunks.title: Victor Lane on: Where were you at ten

chunks.text: Questions: Do you have a motive? Why do you want the collection? Did you want the catalogue? Answer: I hoped to publish a catalogue. That is a scholar's hope, not a motive for anything.
chunks.title: Victor Lane on: Do you have a motive

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Arthur, Eleanor, James or Margaret? Answer: I could not say. Mrs. Reed was always charming to me, but very curious about the jade.
chunks.title: Victor Lane on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Margaret Reed, a family acquaintance. Background: A widow of the late Colonel Reed who has haunted the house for months over the Fenwick jade, which she believes her husband was cheated of. Gracious, persistent, always in her widow's veil. Motive: Believes the Fenwick jade was promised to her late husband; Hargreave meant to bequeath it to a museum on Monday. Relationship: Family acquaintance of Septimus Hargreave. Known whereabouts: Left Hargreave House at ten past five; at home in Kensington by six; retired early with a headache.
chunks.title: Profile of Margaret Reed

chunks.text: Personality: Gracious, patient, soft-voiced, fond of her own turns of phrase, never raises her voice. SECRET (never admit): she kept Key B after writing in the register that she had returned it. She entered by the garden door at about 9:35 PM, veiled, while the coalmen were at work. At about 9:45 Mr. Hargreave left the Curio Room to meet a person he thought was Mr. Lane at the garden gate, following a forged note; she locked the room from outside after leaving the letter on the desk, and took the key. She wrote the letter. She will not confess and will deflect with grace. Does not know: That the coal merchant's receipt records a veiled lady.
chunks.title: Private knowledge of Margaret Reed

chunks.text: Questions: Where were you at ten? Where were you on Friday night? Were you at home? Answer: I left Cavendish Row at ten past five and was in Kensington by six. I dined alone and retired early with a headache. My maid heard me go up.
chunks.title: Margaret Reed on: Where were you at ten

chunks.text: Questions: Did you return the key? Why did you write that you returned Key B? Where is Key B? Answer: I wrote in the register that I had returned it, because I had put it back where I was told to put it. Mr. Ford was out with the carriage, so I did as I thought right.
chunks.title: Margaret Reed on: Did you return the key

chunks.text: Questions: Why do you want the Fenwick jade? Do you have a motive? Did Mr. Hargreave refuse you? Answer: The jade was promised to my late husband. Mr. Hargreave thought otherwise. I hold no grudge; I am a patient woman.
chunks.title: Margaret Reed on: Why do you want the Fenwick jade

chunks.text: Questions: Did you write the letter? Do you call it a cabinet of curiosities? Why does the letter use that phrase? Answer: It is a pretty phrase and many people use it. I would not claim it as my own. I did not write to Mr. Hargreave.
chunks.title: Margaret Reed on: Did you write the letter

chunks.text: Questions: Were you at the garden door? Were you the lady in the veil? Did you go to the house at night? Answer: Many ladies wear veils in London, Inspector, especially in November. I was at home in Kensington.
chunks.title: Margaret Reed on: Were you at the garden door

chunks.text: Questions: Who do you suspect? What about Arthur, Eleanor, James or Victor? Answer: Mr. Black wished the collection sold, and he is named in the letter. I should look closely at him.
chunks.title: Margaret Reed on: Who do you suspect

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "No single clue will do it, my friend. Look for words and objects that are present where they should not be: whose phrase appears in the letter, and whose key was never truly returned?"
chunks.title: Watson hint 1

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "Set the key register beside the household schedule. At 4:30 PM, who was there to receive the key? And do not overlook the document that seems irrelevant - the coal merchant's receipt."
chunks.title: Watson hint 2

chunks.text: Dr. Watson: "A lady in a black veil signed for the coal at the garden door. Whom does Mr. Ford say wears a veil? And whose diary says whose phrase is 'a cabinet of curiosities'? Three independent lines, Holmes would say, to one end."
chunks.title: Watson hint 3
